label: thm:ifandonlyif
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:ifandonlyif}
A three-dimensional Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ admits a complex generalized spin-c Killing spinor with complex Killing function $i\mu-\alpha$ if and only if it is a trans-Sasakian manifold of type $(\alpha,\mu)$ such that the one-form $\mu\zeta$ is exact.
head: environment

label: thm:completeReebnogo
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:completeReebnogo}
Let $(M,g,\varphi,\xi,\zeta)$ be a connected three-dimensional trans-Sasakian manifold of type $(\alpha,\mu)$. Assume that the one-form $\mu\zeta$ is closed and that the characteristic vector field $\xi$ is complete. Then either $\alpha\equiv0$ or $\mu\equiv0$ everywhere on $M$.

title: Remark
body_md: It is well-known that every orientable manifold $M$ of dimension two or three admits a spin structure. However, a spin-c structure on $M$ reduces to a spin structure if and only if the characteristic complex line bundle $\mathcal{L}$ is trivial. Even when $\mathcal{L}$ is trivial, the connection one-form $A$ on $\mathcal{L}$ may have non-trivial holonomy. In that case, the connection $\nabla^{g,A}$ does not reduce to the lift of the Levi-Civita connection $\nabla^g$.

title: Remark
body_md:
Let $\mathrm{d}_A$ denote the covariant exterior derivative and let $\mathrm{d}_A^*$ denote its formal adjoint for the induced $L^2$ Hermitian pairing, tested on compactly supported forms. Since $M$ has real dimension two and $A$ is unitary, $\mathrm{d}_A^{\ast} = - \ast \mathrm{d}_A \ast$. Alternating and taking the negative trace of the second covariant equation yields:
\begin{equation*} 
\mathrm{d}_Ac=(\mu+i\alpha)\theta,\qquad
\mathrm{d}_A\theta=0,\qquad
\mathrm{d}_A^*\theta=-2(\mu+i\alpha)c
\end{equation*}

as a consequence of~\eqref{eq:surfacecovariant}.

label: eq:surfacerealsystem
title: Proposition
body_md:
The real triple $(N, s, v)$ associated with a generalized Killing spinor on $(M,g)$ with Killing function $i\mu-\alpha$ satisfies the differential system:
\begin{gather}
\mathrm{d} N=4\mu v,\qquad \mathrm{d} s=4\alpha*v,\qquad \mathrm{d} |c|^2=2N\mu\, v - 2s\alpha*v,
\label{eq:surfacerealsystem}\\
4 \nabla^g v=\mu N g + \alpha s\, \mathrm{vol}_g,\qquad 4 \nabla^g *v=\mu N \,\mathrm{vol}_g - \alpha s\,g,
\label{eq:nabla-v}\\
2 \mathscr{L}_{v^\sharp}g=\mu N g,\qquad 2 \mathscr{L}_{(*v)^\sharp}g=- \alpha s g, \qquad 2 \mathrm{d} v=\alpha s \mathrm{vol}_g, \qquad 2\mathrm{d} (*v)=\mu N \mathrm{vol}_g,
\label{eq:Lie-dd-v}\\
[v^\sharp,(*v)^\sharp]=0,\qquad \mathrm{d} N((*v)^\sharp)=0,\qquad \mathrm{d} s(v^\sharp)=0.
\label{eq:surfaceconformalfields}
\end{gather}

label: prop:surfaceregularorbit
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:surfaceregularorbit}
Let $(N, s, v)$ be the real triple associated with a generalized Killing spinor on a complete Riemannian surface $(M,g)$. Then, on the universal cover $\widetilde{M^\circ}$, there are global coordinates $(x,y)\in I\times\mathbb R\subset\mathbb R ^2$ satisfying~\eqref{eq:dx-dy}--\eqref{eq:surfacelocalconnection} for the real triple $(\widetilde{N},\widetilde{s},\widetilde{v})$. Furthermore, the deck transformation group $\Lambda$ acts by translation on those coordinates and is therefore identified with a discrete subgroup of $(\mathbb R ^2, +)$. In particular, if $I\neq\mathbb R$, then $\Lambda$ must be vertical.

label: prop:surfacefilledends
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Each point of the closed discrete zero locus of $c$ has a punctured disk neighborhood and determines a distinct end of $M^\circ$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:surfaceregularorbit}, the regular locus $M^{\circ}$ is topologically a plane, a cylinder, or a torus, with one, two, or zero ends, respectively. Thus, there are at most two zeros and, by the hypothesis, at least one zero, which rules out that $M^\circ$ is topologically a torus.\medskip

First, we prove that $M^\circ$ cannot be diffeomorphic to a plane. If the regular locus were a plane, then $M$ is the one-point compactification of $M^\circ$. In the coordinates $(x,y)$ on this plane, fix $x$ and let $y$ tend to infinity. The resulting points converge to the added point, so continuity implies $N$ is constant. Fixing $y$ and letting $x$ tend to an end point of $I$ similarly makes $s$ constant. Then $16|v|^2=N^2-s^2$ would be a positive constant on the regular locus, contrary to $v=0$ at the added point. We conclude that the regular orbit is a cylinder, and filling one or two ends gives the asserted plane or sphere.\medskip

Since $M^\circ$ is a cylinder, in $(x,y)$-coordinates, the deck transformation group $\Lambda$ is generated by an element $(a_0,b_0)\in \mathbb R^2$. A transverse coordinate on the cylinder is $b_0x-a_0y$. If $a_0\neq0$, then $I=\mathbb R$ and every vertical line escapes to either end. Continuity at a filled end forces $N$ to be constant. Since $\mathrm{d} N=4\mu v$ in~\eqref{eq:surfacerealsystem} and $v\neq 0$ on the regular locus, $\mu=0$ there and hence everywhere. If $b_0\neq0$, horizontal lines similarly force $s$ constant and $\alpha=0$. Both coordinates of the generator cannot be non-zero, because that would make both invariants constant and prevent $|v|$ from tending to zero.\medskip

If $\alpha=0$, by $2 \mathscr{L}_{(*v)^\sharp}g=- \alpha s g$ in~\eqref{eq:Lie-dd-v}, the field $4(*v)^\sharp$ is Killing and periodic. If $\mu=0$, by $2 \mathscr{L}_{v^\sharp}g = \mu N g$ in~\eqref{eq:Lie-dd-v}, $N$ is constant and $4v^\sharp$ is Killing and periodic. Normalize the resulting effective circle action to have period $2\pi$. It is free on the regular cylinder. At a fixed point, its differential has rotation weight $1$ or $-1$: a higher weight would yield a nonidentity isometry fixing that point with identity derivative, which is impossible on a connected Riemannian manifold. Orthogonal geodesics to the orbits give a global radial coordinate on the orbit interval and the metric~\eqref{eq:surfacepolarmetric}. Smoothness at a fixed point gives the stated parity and derivative conditions. In the one-zero case, completeness forces the other radial end to have infinite geodesic length. In the two-zero case, the interval is $[0,L]$ after adding its endpoints.

title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:surface_mixing_completeness}
Completeness does \emph{not} imply $\alpha\mu\equiv0$. It excludes only disjoint-support mixing, meaning $\alpha\mu\equiv0$ with neither coefficient identically zero. The examples include complete regular solutions with $\alpha\mu>0$ everywhere. Topological triviality of the characteristic line does not imply flatness of its connection.

title: Remark
body_md: The condition $\mu\zeta=\mathrm{d} f$ implies that $\alpha\mu\equiv0$. Indeed, on a trans-Sasakian manifold of type $(\alpha,\mu)$ we have $\mathrm{d}\zeta=-2\alpha\omega$ and $\mathrm{d}\omega=2\mu\zeta\wedge\omega$, where $\omega=g(\varphi-,-)$. Taking the exterior derivative of $\mathrm{d} f=\mu\zeta$, and then taking the exterior product with $\zeta$ gives $0=-2\alpha\mu\zeta\wedge\omega$. Since $\zeta\wedge\omega$ is nowhere vanishing, we conclude that $\alpha\mu\equiv0$.

If the Riemannian metric $g$ is complete, then either $\alpha$ is identically zero on $M$, or $\mu$ is identically zero on $M$. In particular, a complete connected $\mu$-exact trans-Sasakian three-manifold cannot have both $\alpha\not\equiv0$ and $\mu\not\equiv0$.
